--- execute: eval: true df-print: paged --- # Plotting your data In this chapter you learn how to plot your data. We start with a few quick plots in base R, and then spend most of the chapter on **ggplot2**, the plotting package of the tidyverse. As always, load the tidyverse and read the data first. This time we need both the growth data and the timecourse data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # load the tidyverse library(tidyverse) # read in the data growth_data <- read_tsv("data/Growth_Data.txt", show_col_types = FALSE) timecourse <- read_tsv("data/Timecourse.txt", show_col_types = FALSE) ``` ::: ## Why plot your data? Plots are not only for papers and presentations. They are one of the best ways to check your data before you run any statistics. Summary numbers can hide a lot. @fig-anscombe shows a famous example: four small data sets with almost the same mean, variance and regression line, but with very different patterns. Only the first one is described well by a straight line. Without plotting, you would never notice. ![Anscombe's quartet: four data sets with almost identical summary statistics and the same regression line (blue). Source: Wikipedia, *Anscombe's quartet*.](../images/anscombe_quartet.png){#fig-anscombe width="70%"} So make it a habit to plot your data first, and look at it. ## Quick plots in base R Base R has its own plotting functions. They are not as flexible as ggplot2, but for a quick look at your data they are often faster to type. You will also see them a lot in other people's code, and we use some of them in the statistics chapter. `plot()` draws a scatter plot. Like `lm()` and `t.test()`, it takes a formula: `y ~ x`, read as "y depends on x", and the data frame with `data`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # root length against shoot weight plot(Rootlength ~ FW_shoot_mg, data = growth_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Plants with a missing root length or shoot weight are simply left out. `hist()` draws a histogram. It takes a single column, which we get with `$`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # distribution of the root length hist(growth_data$Rootlength) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: `boxplot()` draws a boxplot per group: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # root length per nutrient level boxplot(Rootlength ~ Nutrient, data = growth_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: A boxplot summarizes the values of each group: - the thick line in the box is the median: half of the values are above it, half below - the box goes from the first to the third quartile, so it holds the middle 50% of the values - the whiskers (the thin lines) go to the most extreme values that are no further than 1.5 times the height of the box away from the box - values further away are drawn as single points. They are often called outliers, but that does not mean that they are wrong All three functions take arguments for labels, for example `xlab`, `ylab` and `main` (the title): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} boxplot(Rootlength ~ Nutrient, data = growth_data, xlab = "Phosphate level", ylab = "Root length (mm)", main = "Root length") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: For quick checks, this is all you need. For plots with colors, groups and several panels, base R code quickly gets long and hard to read. This is where ggplot2 is much easier. ## Your first ggplot Every ggplot is built from the same parts: 1. `ggplot()` starts the plot. You give it the data frame, and in `aes()` (short for **aesthetics**) you say which column goes on which axis. 2. A **geom** says how to draw the data, for example as points (`geom_point()`), boxes (`geom_boxplot()`) or lines (`geom_line()`). 3. The parts are added to each other with `+`. Each part is a **layer** of the plot. Let's make the same scatter plot as above: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning: Removed 23 rows containing missing values or values outside the scale range (`geom_point()`). ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Notice the warning that starts with "Removed 23 rows containing missing values". ggplot2 leaves out the plants with a missing root length (15) or a missing shoot weight (8), just like base R. But unlike base R, it tells you about it. This is not an error: the plot is still made. Now that we know what the warning means, we hide it in the rest of this chapter with `#| warning: false` at the top of the chunks. Always put the `+` at the end of a line, not at the start of the next one. Otherwise R thinks the plot is finished after the first line. ### Exercise Plot the root length (y-axis) against the condition (x-axis). What is different from the plot above? ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Because `Condition` is text and not a number, ggplot2 makes one column of points per condition. Many points lie on top of each other, so it is hard to see how many plants there are. We fix this later with boxplots and `geom_jitter()`. ::: ## Store and save your plots You can store a plot in an object, like any other result in R. To see the plot, type the name of the object: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} root_shoot_plot <- ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength)) + geom_point() root_shoot_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: `ggsave()` saves a plot to a file. The file type comes from the file name, for example `.pdf`, `.png` or `.svg`. With `width`, `height` and `units` you set the size: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggsave("output_examples/Plot_root_length.pdf", plot = root_shoot_plot, width = 12, height = 10, units = "cm") ``` ::: For figures in a paper or a poster, save your plots as **vector** files, such as pdf or svg. A vector file stores lines and points as shapes, so you can zoom in without losing quality, and you can still change details in programs like Inkscape or Illustrator. Raster files, such as png or jpg, store pixels. They are fine for slides and websites. You can also save the plot that you see in the Plots pane with the **Export** button above the plot. ## Aesthetics: colors, shapes and more So far, we put columns on the x- and y-axis. In `aes()`, you can also link columns to other properties of the plot, for example: - `color`: the color of points and lines - `fill`: the color inside boxes and bars - `shape`: the shape of points - `linetype`: solid, dashed or dotted lines Let's color the points by nutrient level: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength, color = Nutrient)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ggplot2 picks the colors and adds a legend for us. There is an important difference between setting a property **inside** and **outside** `aes()`: - Inside `aes()`, you link the property to a column: each nutrient level gets its own color. - Outside `aes()`, in the geom, you give a fixed value for all points. For example, to make all points blue and a bit transparent (with `alpha`, from 0 for invisible to 1 for solid): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength)) + geom_point(color = "blue", alpha = 0.4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Exercise Make the scatter plot again. Color the points by condition, and give each nutrient level its own shape. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength, color = Condition, shape = Nutrient)) + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: ## Geoms: different types of plots To change the type of plot, you change the geom. Here are the ones you will use most. ### Boxplots ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength)) + geom_boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: A boxplot hides how many plants there are. You can show them by adding the points as a second layer. `geom_jitter()` draws the points with a bit of random sideways noise, so they don't lie on top of each other. With `width` you set how far they spread: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: `outlier.shape = NA` hides the outlier points of the boxplot. Otherwise these plants would be drawn twice: once by the boxplot and once by `geom_jitter()`. With `fill`, we get one box per nutrient level within each condition: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength, fill = Nutrient)) + geom_boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Histograms A histogram only needs the x-axis. ggplot2 counts how many plants fall into each interval (bin). With `binwidth` you set the width of the bins, here 5 mm: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Rootlength)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: To compare the nutrient levels, we fill the bars by nutrient. `position = "identity"` draws the two histograms on top of each other instead of stacking them, and `alpha` makes them transparent, so we can see both: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Rootlength, fill = Nutrient)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, position = "identity", alpha = 0.5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Line plots Line plots are good for measurements over time, like our timecourse data. We don't want a line through every single plant, but through the mean of each group at each time point. So we first summarize the data with `group_by()` and `summarize()`, as in the chapter "Working with the tidyverse": ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # mean root length per nutrient, condition and time point timecourse_summary <- timecourse |> group_by(Nutrient, Condition, Timepoint) |> summarize(mean_root = mean(Rootlength)) |> ungroup() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` `summarise()` has grouped output by 'Nutrient', 'Condition'. You can override using the `.groups` argument. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} timecourse_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Let's plot the plants grown with low phosphate. `color = Condition` gives us one line per condition, and we add the points on top of the lines: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} timecourse_summary |> filter(Nutrient == "low_P") |> ggplot(aes(x = Timepoint, y = mean_root, color = Condition)) + geom_line() + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Notice that we can give the result of a pipe straight to `ggplot()`. After `ggplot()`, the layers are joined with `+`, not with `|>`. ### Trend lines `geom_smooth()` adds a trend line to a scatter plot. With `method = "lm"` it draws the straight line of a linear model, which you will learn about in the statistics chapter. The grey band shows how uncertain the line is: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: If you color by a column, you get one line per group: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = FW_shoot_mg, y = Rootlength, color = Nutrient)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + geom_smooth(method = "lm") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Exercise 1. Make a boxplot of the shoot weight per condition, with the plants shown as points. 2. Make a line plot of the timecourse for the plants grown with **high** phosphate. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # 1. shoot weight per condition ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = FW_shoot_mg)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # 2. timecourse with high phosphate timecourse_summary |> filter(Nutrient == "high_P") |> ggplot(aes(x = Timepoint, y = mean_root, color = Condition)) + geom_line() + geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-2.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: ## Bar graphs with error bars In biology, you often see bar graphs that show the mean of each group with error bars. For this, we first make a table with the mean and the standard deviation of each group. The **standard deviation** (sd) describes how much the root length varies between the plants of a group: the larger it is, the more the plants differ from each other. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # mean and standard deviation of the root length per treatment root_summary <- growth_data |> group_by(Nutrient, Condition) |> summarize(mean_root = mean(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE), sd_root = sd(Rootlength, na.rm = TRUE)) |> ungroup() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` `summarise()` has grouped output by 'Nutrient'. You can override using the `.groups` argument. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} root_summary ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: `geom_col()` draws bars with the height that is given in the data. `geom_errorbar()` draws the error bars, from `ymin` to `ymax`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(root_summary, aes(x = Condition, y = mean_root, fill = Nutrient)) + geom_col(position = position_dodge()) + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_root - sd_root, ymax = mean_root + sd_root), position = position_dodge(width = 0.9), width = 0.2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: `position_dodge()` puts the bars of the two nutrient levels next to each other instead of on top of each other. The error bars need the same dodge, so that they end up on top of the right bar. ::: callout-important ## What do the error bars show? Error bars can show different things: the standard deviation, the **standard error** of the mean, or a confidence interval. These can differ a lot in size for the same data, so a reader can only interpret your error bars if you say which one you use. Always write it in the figure legend, for example "mean ± sd". The statistics chapter shows how large the difference between sd and se can be. ::: A bar graph only shows the mean of each group and hides everything else. A boxplot with the points, as above, shows how the plants are spread and how many there are. Think about which plot tells your reader more. ## Order of the groups ggplot2 sorts text columns alphabetically. That is why `129E` and `13C` come before `mock`, and `high_P` before `low_P`. Often you want another order, for example with the control first. Remember factors from the chapter "Data objects"? The order of the levels sets the order in the plot. With `mutate()` and `factor()`, we set the order ourselves: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} growth_data <- growth_data |> mutate(Condition = factor(Condition, levels = c("mock", "129E", "13C")), Nutrient = factor(Nutrient, levels = c("low_P", "high_P"))) ``` ::: Now the control comes first, and low phosphate before high phosphate: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength, fill = Nutrient)) + geom_boxplot() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-26-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## Facets: one panel per group Sometimes a plot gets clearer if you split it into several panels, one per group. This is called **faceting**. `facet_wrap()` makes one panel for each value of a column. The `~` reads as "by": ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength)) + geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) + geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3) + facet_wrap(~ Nutrient) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-27-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: By default, all panels have the same axes, which makes it easy to compare them. With `scales = "free_y"`, each panel gets its own y-axis. And with `ncol` or `nrow` you set how the panels are arranged. ### Exercise Plot the timecourse for both nutrient levels, with one panel per nutrient level. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(timecourse_summary, aes(x = Timepoint, y = mean_root, color = Condition)) + geom_line() + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~ Nutrient) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: ## Labels, colors and themes The default plots are good for a first look. For a report or a paper, you usually want better labels, your own colors and a cleaner look. - `labs()` sets the axis titles, the legend title and a plot title. - `scale_fill_manual()` sets your own colors for `fill` (and `scale_color_manual()` for `color`). You can name the colors, so that each group gets the right one. - A **theme** sets the overall look. `theme_classic()` has no grey background and no grid lines. Other built-in themes are, for example, `theme_bw()` and `theme_minimal()`. - `theme()` changes single parts of the plot, for example where the legend goes. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} root_plot <- ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = Rootlength, fill = Nutrient)) + geom_boxplot() + scale_fill_manual(values = c(low_P = "grey80", high_P = "grey30")) + labs(x = "Condition", y = "Root length (mm)", fill = "Phosphate") + theme_classic() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") root_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Colors can be given by name, like `"grey80"`, or as a hex code, like `"#2A6FDB"`. Choose colors that people with color blindness can tell apart, and that still work when printed in grey. ## Combine several plots For a figure with several panels, you can combine plots with `ggarrange()` from the ggpubr package. Install it once with `install.packages("ggpubr")` in the Console. We also use ggpubr in the statistics chapter. Let's make a second plot for the shoot weight, with the same look: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} shoot_plot <- ggplot(growth_data, aes(x = Condition, y = FW_shoot_mg, fill = Nutrient)) + geom_boxplot() + scale_fill_manual(values = c(low_P = "grey80", high_P = "grey30")) + labs(x = "Condition", y = "Shoot fresh weight (mg)", fill = "Phosphate") + theme_classic() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: `ggarrange()` takes the plots, labels for the panels, and the number of columns and rows. `common.legend = TRUE` shows the legend only once: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggpubr) combined_plot <- ggarrange(root_plot, shoot_plot, labels = c("A", "B"), ncol = 2, nrow = 1, common.legend = TRUE, legend = "bottom") combined_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](plotting_basics_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-31-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: You save it with `ggsave()`, as any other plot: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggsave("output_examples/Two_plots.pdf", plot = combined_plot, width = 18, height = 10, units = "cm") ``` ::: ## Summary In this chapter you learned how to: - make quick plots in base R with `plot()`, `hist()` and `boxplot()` - build a ggplot from data, `aes()` and geoms, joined with `+` - store plots in objects and save them with `ggsave()` - link columns to colors, fills and shapes in `aes()`, or set fixed values outside `aes()` - make scatter plots, boxplots, histograms, line plots, trend lines and bar graphs with error bars - set the order of groups with factor levels - split a plot into panels with `facet_wrap()` - change labels, colors and the theme - combine several plots with `ggarrange()` ## Further reading - [An introduction into ggplot](https://ndombrowski.github.io/Ggplot_tutorial/): a tutorial with more examples and exercises, on a different data set (penguins). It goes deeper into topics that we only touched here, such as position adjustments, scales and axes, themes, and packages that extend ggplot2. - The [ggplot2 website](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) lists all geoms and functions, with examples.
